content: Seven of the eleven studies conducted point-of-care (POC) testing outside of laboratory settings. One study specifically compared internal quality control rates and the return of test results to caregivers for infant samples tested using POC technology, as performed by nurses versus laboratory-trained personnel. This comparison aimed to evaluate the impact of task-sharing on the quality of testing. POC same-day testing significantly reduced the time required to deliver test results to caregivers. Across all seven studies, the median time between sample collection and caregivers receiving results was zero days (95% CI: 0–0 days), regardless of the test type, the infant's age, or the healthcare facility type. Same-day results were achieved 97% of the time with POC testing, compared to 0% with standard care. For laboratory-based testing, the median time for caregivers to receive results ranged from 8 to 125 days, with a median of 35 days (95% CI: 35–37 days). In five of the seven studies, the median time exceeded 30 days for laboratory-based testing. Three studies evaluated the performance of cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assays when used by non-laboratory personnel. In two of these studies, non-laboratory personnel achieved 100% sensitivity and specificity in identifying cryptococcal antigen. In the third study, when tested on serum samples, the assays demonstrated a sensitivity of 93% (95% CI: 66–100%) and specificity of 100% (95% CI: 88–100%). When trained nurses performed cryptococcal antigen lateral flow assays at the POC, the testing was feasible, highly accurate on serum specimens, and had the potential to accelerate prophylaxis and treatment for HIV-associated cryptococcal infections. Nurses also successfully tested external quality assurance panels using syphilis rapid tests, achieving sensitivity and specificity exceeding 90%. Three studies compared the performance of alanine aminotransferase (ALT) and hemoglobin enumeration tests operated by non-laboratory personnel with laboratory-based technologies operated by laboratory professionals. Non-laboratory personnel performed these tests comparably to laboratory-based technologies. A semi-quantitative, visual POC ALT assay performed by nurses showed a sensitivity of 87% and specificity of 77% compared to laboratory-based methods. One study reviewed the performance of creatinine and lactate testing by non-laboratory personnel at two clinics, demonstrating feasibility and clinical utility. Using POC viral load tests, same-day results were available to clinicians 99% of the time (median time: 0 days) and to patients 99% of the time (median: 0 days). In contrast, with standard laboratory-based testing, same-day results were available to clinicians less than 25% of the time (median: 2 days) and to patients less than 1% of the time (median: 28 days). Observational studies highlighted significantly shorter times to return results to both clinicians and patients with POC testing compared to laboratory-based testing. The estimated time to clinical action, such as enhanced adherence counseling or initiating second-line antiretroviral therapy (ART), was also shorter following POC testing. The Guideline Development Group strongly recommended POC testing based on its overwhelming benefits, including rapid testing, faster return of results to clinicians and patients, and quicker clinical action. POC testing also reduced the number of healthcare visits required for caregivers to receive results and ensured more reliable timing of results. While no major harms were identified, the intervention required extensive network support and maintenance. Task-sharing of specimen collection and POC testing with non-laboratory personnel was found to be feasible, cost-effective, and acceptable. Deploying less-trained personnel for diagnostic testing and sample collection could save costs, with the primary expenses being training, supervision, and remuneration. Decentralization would likely increase the proportion of non-laboratory personnel required for specimen collection and testing, necessitating careful assessment and expansion of human resource capacity. Task-sharing and decentralization are expected to improve equity by increasing access to testing for rural populations and key populations who face barriers to traditional healthcare services. Decentralized testing, particularly with same-day result technologies, could enhance diagnostic access. A systematic review in 2019 found that 58% of non-laboratory personnel found preparing dried blood spot specimens for viral load testing very easy, 43% found specimen collection easy, and 85% deemed the process suitable for non-laboratory personnel. Nurses in South Africa achieved a 98% success rate in finger-prick blood specimen collection. Diagnostic integration, combining laboratory-based and POC technologies, is critical for expanding access to high-quality diagnostic testing. This approach requires centralized support from national laboratories and programs to ensure adequate training, mentorship, quality assurance, and data accuracy. Expanding human resource capacity and addressing legal and regulatory issues are also essential. WHO has developed tools and guidelines to address health workforce dynamics and recommends systematic approaches to workload assessment among healthcare providers. Research gaps remain, particularly in diagnostic accuracy studies comparing newer POC technologies operated by non-laboratory personnel versus laboratory professionals. Good practice statements emphasize the need for balanced integration of diagnostic services across disease programs, particularly for HIV and tuberculosis (TB). Diagnostic integration optimizes resource use, improves care pathways, and enhances access for underserved populations. Several countries are already implementing diagnostic integration, sharing devices, and incorporating testing for multiple diseases, such as HIV, TB, hepatitis, and emerging infections. Careful planning and coordination are essential for program management and service delivery. Diagnostic integration and device sharing can reduce costs across assays, diseases, and programs by increasing test volumes and optimizing device utilization. Challenges include adjusting laboratory and clinic workflows, ensuring same-day result return for urgent tests, and managing additional patient demand. Expanding access to high-quality diagnostic testing requires attention to human resources, supply chains, quality assurance, and regulatory components to build sustainable and integrated networks.
